source.title: Breaking Bad Tokens: Detoxification of LLMs Using Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Agam Goyal; Vedant Rathi; W. Yeh; Yian Wang; Yuen Chen; Hari Sundaram

page_placements.theme: Whether one latent captures a concept depends on width (and layer); multi-latent composites recover it

record.tranche_reason: Reports that toxic features in the wider Gemma SAE fragmented and that using those features for detoxification performed worse than using the narrower SAE; a summed-vector intervention largely reduced that performance gap. It does not directly measure feature-input partitions or geometric similarity.
record.gate_note: Only the feature-splitting experiment bears on the claim. The toxicity reductions elsewhere, fluency and capability evaluations, and the threshold sweep do not measure splitting. The paper's stated fragmentation is not accompanied by direct input-coverage or direction-matching measurements.
record.test_reason: The study assumes feature splitting and uses it to explain a gap in detoxification performance between 16K and 65K GemmaScope SAEs on Gemma-2-2B. It never measures splitting itself. It does not match features across widths, check whether finer latents cover a coarse latent's inputs, or compare decoder directions. The only numbers are toxicity scores under steering, a downstream steering-efficacy measure rather than the splitting structure V1–V6 describe. The statement that toxic features 'fragmented across several narrower definitions' is asserted without a reported measurement. The summed-decoder recovery fits children summing near a parent direction, but no direction or coverage was measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that feature splitting in wider SAEs hampers SAE-based detoxification, and that greater width does not guarantee better steering. Composing the 65K SAE's toxic-feature vectors makes it nearly as effective as the 16K SAE. The attribution to splitting is the authors' interpretation of a toxicity gap, not a direct measurement of splitting.
record.recipe_differences: Uses existing 16K and 65K GemmaScope SAEs, selects toxic features, and compares their constant-steering detoxification outcomes; it does not match features across widths or measure input partitions or direction similarity.
record.method_sensitivity: SAE width (16K vs 65K); the reported difference is averaged across layers 10 and 20 and steering strengths. The summed-vector composition changes the reported gap.

fits_no_version.finding: Constant steering with the best toxic feature from the 65K GemmaScope SAE gave toxicity 0.062 higher on average than the 16K SAE. Steering with the summed 65K toxic-feature decoder vectors cut the gap to 0.01.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wider SAEs can yield individual features that are less effective single-feature steering vectors for a coarse concept; composing several wide-SAE features recovers efficacy.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP), 2025
record.problems: The width comparison uses one model and two SAE widths. The splitting experiment reports aggregate toxicity differences across layers and steering strengths, without uncertainty estimates or direct measurements of feature matching, input coverage, or directional geometry.
record.rows_left_out: No other feature-splitting outcomes are reported separately. The paper's other toxicity, fluency, and capability results do not measure the claim's feature-splitting structure.

untested.parts: All of it: no cross-width feature matching, input-coverage or direction-similarity measurement.
All of it: GemmaScope 16K vs 65K is used, but splitting is not measured.
Feature families, geometry and hierarchy are not examined.
Decomposition of larger latents into smaller ones and novel latents are not examined.
Training objectives are not compared; the authors only speculate about disentanglement-oriented training.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T5' and V1/V2 links are downgraded. The only evidence is a steering-efficacy difference across widths, a related but different construct. The paper cites Towards Monosemanticity and Leask et al. as background; neither is re-tested.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports fragmentation across SAE widths, but does not directly test whether child features partition the coarse feature's inputs or lie near its direction.
Tests two widths of GemmaScope on Gemma-2-2B only; it does not establish the pattern across large models, multiple model families, or SAE releases generally.
Nested feature families, geometric closeness, and correspondence to a conceptual hierarchy are not tested.
Parent-child co-firing, absorption, and the effect of changing SAE size or sparsity on absorption are not tested.
Decomposition of larger latents into smaller latents, novel latents, and completeness or atomicity across dictionary sizes are not tested.
The study does not test whether splitting is caused by the SAE objective or compare objectives such as Matryoshka SAEs.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Compared constant steering with best-performing toxic features from 16K and 65K GemmaScope SAEs.
rows.measure: Average toxicity score of generations under constant steering
rows.baseline: 16K SAE constant steering; absolute toxicity value not stated
rows.value: 65K SAE interventions had toxicity scores 0.062 higher on average across steering strengths and both layers.
rows.note: The text attributes the difference to wider-SAE feature splitting and says individual toxic features fragmented across narrower definitions. The toxicity measure does not establish input coverage or geometric proximity.
rows.check: Measures toxicity after steering with the single best feature from each SAE width, not feature splitting. The 0.062 gap is attributed to splitting but could reflect feature selection (top-3 by activation difference, best single feature) or steering-factor scaling. Baseline absolute value is not given.

source_check.problem: none; 65K best-feature constant steering gives toxicity 0.062 higher on average across strengths and layers 10 and 20 than 16K; cannot_determine fits since toxicity cannot show splitting

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Applied constant steering using the summed decoder vectors of the 65K SAE's toxic features, scaled by their average steering factor.
rows.measure: Difference in average toxicity scores between wider- and narrower-SAE interventions
rows.value: Composition-based steering reduced the difference to 0.01 while maintaining fluency.
rows.note: This is a post-hoc mitigation of the detoxification-performance difference, not a direct test of whether the features partition inputs or have nearby directions.
rows.check: Post-hoc mitigation of the steering gap (0.062 to 0.01) by summing the 65K toxic-feature decoder vectors. This is a downstream steering result. It does not measure whether those features partition a 16K feature's inputs or lie near its direction.

source_check.problem: none; summed 65K toxic-feature decoder vectors scaled by average steering factor cut the difference to 0.01, fluency maintained

relation.reason: The paper uses splitting as a design tool (two widths 'to study feature splitting effects'; summed 65K toxic-feature vectors as mitigation) without testing it. This matches uses_without_test and T4.

tranche.reason: No splitting measurement: no cross-width matching, input coverage or decoder similarity. It uses the splitting idea to motivate two SAE widths and build a summed-decoder mitigation, and reports only steering toxicity/fluency. That fits T4, not T3 or T5.

source_check.notes: The splitting attribution is the authors' interpretation of a toxicity gap. Features are top-3 per layer by mean absolute activation difference on ParaDetox toxic/non-toxic pairs, and constant steering reports the single best feature. Nothing shows that 65K features partition a 16K feature's inputs. Rows are correctly unlinked (versions none).

statements.problem: None. 0.062 and 0.01 match Section 4.4 (Gemma-2-2B, GemmaScope 16K vs 65K, constant steering, averaged across steering strengths and layers 10 and 20).
